title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Floral Diversity — 2025
origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 floral diversity unit

questions.question: Name the three domains of life and state the rules of binomial nomenclature with one example.
questions.solution:
The three domains are Archaea (prokaryotes of extreme habitats, with ether-linked membrane lipids and no peptidoglycan), Bacteria (prokaryotes with peptidoglycan walls) and Eukarya (nucleus and membrane-bound organelles).
Binomial nomenclature, given by Linnaeus, names every organism with two Latinised words: the genus with a capital letter and the species in lower case, both italicised in print and underlined when handwritten, e.g. Mangifera indica for mango. The name is Latin, follows the rule of priority, and is the same worldwide, which is why scientific names avoid the confusion of local names.

questions.question: State the basis of Whittaker's five kingdom classification, name the kingdoms with one example each, and give one merit and one demerit of the system.
questions.solution:
Basis: cell structure (prokaryote or eukaryote), thallus organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.
Kingdoms: Monera (bacteria), Protista (Euglena), Fungi (Rhizopus), Plantae (mango), Animalia (earthworm).
Merit: it separates prokaryotes from eukaryotes and autotrophs from heterotrophs, placing fungi in a kingdom of their own. Demerit: Protista and Fungi remain heterogeneous groups, and bacteria and cyanobacteria are kept together although they differ greatly.

questions.question: Give the diagnostic features of the four classes of fungi with one example each.
questions.solution:
Phycomycetes: aseptate, coenocytic hyphae, spores non-motile or motile; Rhizopus and Mucor.
Ascomycetes (sac fungi): septate hyphae, sexual spores as ascospores inside an ascus, often budding; Penicillium, yeast.
Basidiomycetes (club fungi): septate hyphae, basidiospores borne on a basidium; mushroom Agaricus, puffball.
Deuteromycetes (fungi imperfecti): septate hyphae, only asexual reproduction by conidia, sexual stage unknown; Alternaria, Trichoderma.

questions.question: Describe reproduction in Mucor and in yeast.
questions.solution:
Mucor reproduces vegetatively by fragmentation of the mycelium, asexually by non-motile sporangiospores formed inside a sporangium on a sporangiophore, and sexually by conjugation of two opposite strains: gametangia fuse, a thick-walled zygospore forms, undergoes meiosis and germinates into a new mycelium.
Yeast (Saccharomyces) multiplies mainly by budding — a small bud grows out, receives a nucleus and separates — and sometimes by fission. Sexually two haploid cells fuse and the diploid cell undergoes meiosis to form four ascospores inside an ascus.

questions.question: How are edible mushrooms distinguished from poisonous ones, and what is the economic importance of fungi?
questions.solution:
There is no single reliable field test. Edible forms such as Agaricus campestris and Pleurotus (oyster) are identified by species; deadly ones such as Amanita phalloides and A. muscaria carry amatoxins and must never be eaten. Warnings are only hints, not proof — never judge by colour, ring or volva alone.
Economic importance: food rich in protein and B vitamins, flavour and enzymes, antibiotics (penicillin), organic acids, vitamins, mycorrhizal partners for crops, decomposers that recycle nutrients and yeasts for bakery and brewing; on the other hand fungi spoil food, rot timber and cause crop and skin diseases.

questions.question: What is a lichen? Name its two partners and state why lichens are used as pollution indicators.
questions.solution:
A lichen is a symbiotic association of a fungus (mycobiont) and an alga or cyanobacterium (phycobiont). The fungus provides shelter, water and minerals; the alga photosynthesises and supplies food.
Lichens absorb water and gases directly over their whole surface and have no protective cuticle, so they accumulate sulphur dioxide and other pollutants and die or change form when air is polluted. Their presence therefore indicates clean air and their disappearance indicates pollution.

questions.question: Give the characteristic pigments and reserve foods of green, brown and red algae, and describe reproduction in Spirogyra.
questions.solution:
Chlorophyceae (green): chlorophyll a and b, reserve starch. Phaeophyceae (brown): chlorophyll a and c with fucoxanthin, reserve laminarin and mannitol. Rhodophyceae (red): chlorophyll a and d with phycoerythrin, reserve floridean starch.
Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga with spiral chloroplasts. It multiplies asexually by fragmentation; sexually it reproduces by conjugation — in scalariform conjugation two filaments lie side by side and form a conjugation tube through which one gamete passes, and in lateral conjugation gametes of adjacent cells fuse. The zygote becomes a zygospore, undergoes meiosis and germinates into a new filament.

questions.question: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom? Describe the structure and reproduction of Marchantia.
questions.solution:
Bryophytes live on land but need a film of water for the male gametes to swim to the archegonia, so they are called amphibians of the plant kingdom. The gametophyte is the dominant plant, vascular tissue is absent, and the sporophyte is dependent on the gametophyte.
Marchantia has a dorsiventral thallus with a midrib, rhizoids and scales below, and pores on the upper surface. It reproduces asexually by gemmae formed in gemma cups, and sexually by antheridia and archegonia borne on umbrella-shaped gametophores; water carries the sperm, the zygote becomes a sporophyte whose capsule releases spores.

questions.question: State the distinguishing features of pteridophytes and describe the life cycle of Dryopteris.
questions.solution:
Pteridophytes are the first true vascular plants: the sporophyte is dominant with true roots, stem and compound leaves, and spores are produced in sporangia, so they never form seeds.
In Dryopteris the sporophyte has a rhizome and large fronds whose underside bears sori with sporangia. Spores fall on damp soil and grow into a heart-shaped prothallus (gametophyte) bearing antheridia and archegonia; water carries the sperm to the egg, the zygote develops into a new sporophyte, and the prothallus dies — a clear alternation of generations.

questions.question: Why are gymnosperms called naked-seeded plants? Describe reproduction in Pinus and give two economic uses.
questions.solution:
Their ovules lie exposed on the megasporophylls of a cone, and after fertilisation the seeds remain uncovered on the cone scales because there is no ovary to enclose them.
Pinus is monoecious and heterosporous. Male cones bear microsporophylls producing pollen with air sacs that is carried by wind; female cones bear ovules with archegonia. Pollination occurs when pollen reaches the ovule, but fertilisation follows about a year later; the zygote develops into an embryo and the whole structure becomes a winged seed between the scale.
Uses: timber and pulp, resin, turpentine and rosin, and edible seeds (chilgoza from Pinus gerardiana).

questions.question: Give four differences between a root and a stem, and name one modification of each with the plant.
questions.solution:
1. Position: the root grows downwards under the soil, the stem grows upwards into air.
2. Nodes and internodes: absent in the root, present in the stem.
3. Leaves and buds: the root bears neither, the stem bears both.
4. Branching and geotropism: root branching is endogenous and negatively phototropic; stem branching is exogenous and positively phototropic.
Modifications: the tap root of carrot is swollen for food storage; the stem of potato becomes an underground tuber while that of cucumber becomes a tendril for climbing.

questions.question: Write the taxonomic hierarchy and give the floral formula, one diagnostic flower character and one example of the families Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae.
questions.solution:
Hierarchy: Kingdom → Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
Brassicaceae: Br, ⊕, K 2+2, C 4, A 2+4, G(2); tetradynamous stamens and a siliqua fruit; Brassica campestris.
Fabaceae: Br, %, K(5), C 1+2+(2), A(9)+1, G 1; papilionaceous corolla and a legume pod with root nodules; Pisum sativum.
Solanaceae: Br, ⊕, K(5), C(5), A 5, G(2); persistent calyx with axile placentation and a berry or capsule; Solanum tuberosum.
Liliaceae: Br, ⊕, P 3+3, A 3+3, G(3); trimerous perianth with a superior ovary; Allium cepa.
